title: Training Day

jokes.text: Michael and D'Angelo making increasingly absurd toasts at the bar: 'To beginnings and endings.' / 'And to middles, the unsung heroes.' / 'And to moms.' / 'To moms of the troops.'
jokes.setup: Two strangers bond over drinks and make sincere toasts to life milestones
jokes.punchline: The toasts escalate into increasingly nonsensical territory — 'middles, the unsung heroes' and then the non-sequitur 'moms of the troops'
jokes.explanation: The escalating toasts perfectly capture Michael's brand of earnest absurdity — he's not trying to be funny, he's deeply sincere about 'middles.' The escalation structure is clean and the payoff of 'moms of the troops' is a genuinely odd non-sequitur that lands because of how committed both men are to it.

jokes.text: Do not tell my fiancée I'm drinking on a Wednesday. / I won't. / I don't know her.
jokes.setup: Michael asks D'Angelo not to tell his fiancée he's drinking on a Wednesday, as if D'Angelo has any connection to her
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's 'I don't know her' — a perfectly logical but completely deflating non-sequitur that punctures Michael's dramatic request
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured three-line exchange. The joke works because Michael's request is already slightly absurd (asking a stranger to keep a secret from someone they've never met), and D'Angelo's response is the most literal, logical possible reply — which makes it devastating. Perfect economy; every word earns its place. The 'I don't know her' lands hard because it exposes the absurdity of Michael's social anxiety without a single wasted syllable.

jokes.text: No, no, I don't want to end up like Sonny Bobo.
jokes.setup: D'Angelo asks if Michael is doing any skiing in Colorado
jokes.punchline: Michael declines, citing the ski death of Sonny Bono — calling him 'Sonny Bobo,' a slight name mangling
jokes.explanation: The name mangling ('Bobo' instead of 'Bono') is classic Michael — he's almost right but not quite. The dark reference to Sonny Bono's death is delivered with complete earnestness, and the bartender's straight-faced 'that's just good sense right there' elevates it further.

jokes.text: Yeah, everyone I know who skis is dead.
jokes.setup: Michael says he doesn't want to end up like Sonny Bono, implying skiing is dangerous
jokes.punchline: He escalates to the absurd logical conclusion that EVERYONE he knows who skis has died — delivered as a casual observation
jokes.explanation: This line does a lot of work in seven words. The absurd dark logic — implying his social circle has been devastated by skiing fatalities — is quintessential Michael Scott obliviousness. The deadpan delivery makes it funnier; he's not performing the line, he's reporting a fact. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I actually tried to get an animal Olympics going. / Really? What happened? / You know, life happened.
jokes.setup: Michael mentions he's an Olympics nut, suggesting a shared interest with D'Angelo
jokes.punchline: He reveals he tried to organize an 'animal Olympics' — and the project failed not due to logistics but simply because 'life happened,' a phrase that implies this was a serious adult endeavor
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of a Michael Scott joke. 'Animal Olympics' is the kind of harebrained scheme that is 100% believable for this character. The kicker — 'life happened' — treats the failure of an animal Olympics with the same gravity as a collapsed marriage or abandoned novel. D'Angelo's straight 'Really? What happened?' makes it land harder. High character integration: this joke could only be Michael Scott.

jokes.text: The extended phone call scene where Michael and D'Angelo realize they are both at the same bar talking to each other in person while on the phone
jokes.setup: Michael calls D'Angelo because he thinks D'Angelo is late; both are at 'the bar in the lobby'
jokes.punchline: They are literally standing next to each other, watching each other's lips move while hearing each other's voices in the phone — a slow-dawning realization played out in excruciating, delightful detail
jokes.explanation: A well-executed classic sitcom bit elevated by commitment. The prolonged confusion — 'I hear your voice in the phone' / 'I see your lips moving' — milks the absurdity perfectly. The slow dawning realization is structured beautifully with each line of dialogue ratcheting up the tension before the reveal. Strong impact because it's visual comedy in a transcript-only scene that still reads as inherently funny.

jokes.text: She'll do. Oh, she'll do just fine. (D'Angelo's first look at the Scranton office)
jokes.setup: Michael proudly presents the Dunder Mifflin Scranton office to D'Angelo
jokes.punchline: 'She'll do' — faint praise, delivered with the quiet resignation of a man who knows he's walked into a mediocre situation
jokes.explanation: A functional joke establishing D'Angelo's understated character. 'She'll do' is not original but lands because it deflates Michael's obvious pride. Sets character tone efficiently.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'It is, uh... it feels like the culmination of a lot of hard work, a lot of good fortune, and, uh...' — interrupted by D'Angelo walking in — 'Did that... did that just happen? We should write a movie or something. I'm serious.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a sincere, emotional confessional about his last day and the arrival of his replacement
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo interrupts the heartfelt moment, and Michael immediately pivots to pitching a movie about their absurd meet-cute — treating a mundane coincidence as Hollywood material
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott self-aggrandizement — taking a mildly funny coincidence and immediately wanting to immortalize it in cinema. The pivot from sincere emotion to movie pitch is very on-brand. Works because of character integration but isn't the sharpest version of this type of joke.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'No, it's not Ashton Kutcher. It's Kevin Malone. Equally handsome, equally smart.'
jokes.setup: The office is speculating about who the new manager is; Kevin does a talking head to clarify
jokes.punchline: Kevin compares himself to Ashton Kutcher in looks and intelligence — a comparison that is clearly, objectively false but delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Pure Kevin Malone: zero self-awareness, maximum confidence. The juxtaposition of 'Ashton Kutcher' with 'Kevin Malone' is inherently funny, and 'equally handsome, equally smart' delivered without irony is perfect character comedy. High character integration — this joke only works coming from Kevin.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Okay, everyone, as you know, one of my favorite things is fanfare for its own sake. So without further ado, let's all start clapping.'
jokes.setup: Michael is introducing D'Angelo to the office and building anticipation
jokes.punchline: He openly admits his motivation is 'fanfare for its own sake' — not celebrating D'Angelo but celebrating the act of celebration — then commands everyone to clap on demand
jokes.explanation: 'Fanfare for its own sake' is a hilariously self-aware phrase for Michael to use — he's actually articulating his own pathology while having zero insight into it. Commanding people to 'start clapping' before the person even arrives is the kind of socially tone-deaf move that is pure Michael.

jokes.text: Michael announces D'Angelo's arrival by asking everyone to start clapping first, then introducing him — a ceremony for its own sake
jokes.setup: Michael says 'one of my favorite things is fanfare for its own sake' and instructs everyone to start clapping before any introduction is made
jokes.punchline: The room claps for an empty hallway, then D'Angelo enters — the spectacle has been engineered entirely to serve Michael's need for drama
jokes.explanation: Michael explicitly naming his own pathology ('fanfare for its own sake') is a funny bit of self-awareness that he doesn't realize is damning. The clapping-before-entry visual gag works well.

jokes.text: D'Angelo's self-introduction: 'Did I want to be made manager? Sure. A great opportunity squandered? Absolutely. A crushing blow? Yes. Will I get over it? Mmm... No. But life goes on.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is introducing himself to his new staff and listing things about himself
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a brutally honest self-assessment of his disappointment at not getting the manager job — delivered as a series of rhetorical Q&As ending in 'No. But life goes on.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is immaculate: a rising series of self-interrogating questions that seem to be building toward resilience — 'Will I get over it? Mmm... No.' The 'Mmm' pause before 'No' is everything. Then 'But life goes on' tacks on a hollow platitude that makes the honesty even funnier. It establishes D'Angelo as a genuinely interesting comic character in under 30 seconds. The Q&A structure, the escalation, the payoff — all exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael's quiet talking head after D'Angelo says 'life goes on': 'Not for me.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo ends his introduction with 'But life goes on' — an optimistic platitude
jokes.punchline: Cut to Michael in a talking head: 'Not for me.' — referring to his impending departure from the company that has been his entire identity
jokes.explanation: Three words. This is the best joke in the episode and one of the show's finest talking-head cuts. The structural perfection — using D'Angelo's optimistic closing line as the setup and cutting to Michael for the punchline — is elegant television writing. It works on multiple levels: it's darkly funny (Michael being dramatic about leaving a paper company), it's emotionally true (his whole identity IS this office), and it's a perfect example of mockumentary form. The economy is unmatched: three words that contain pathos, comedy, and character. This is what an 8+ looks like.

jokes.text: Michael and D'Angelo's meet-cute re-enacted: 'I saw you coming out of the bathroom earlier.' / 'Well, I guess I'm gonna go back to my cave.' / 'Okay. It was really great meeting you.'
jokes.setup: Michael and D'Angelo pretend they didn't recognize each other from the night before and stage a formal meeting for the cameras
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's 'I guess I'm gonna go back to my cave' as a deflection is odd enough, but Michael's 'It was really great meeting you' after a 20-second interaction is the kicker
jokes.explanation: A mild bit of awkward comedy, functional but not exceptional. The 'cave' line is a slightly odd choice that doesn't land as hard as it probably should.

jokes.text: D'Angelo says 'And that is what they call a meet cute.' / Michael then retells the bar story to the office, and D'Angelo says 'That was crazy.'
jokes.setup: Michael is thrilled about his coincidental meeting with D'Angelo and retells it
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo uses the romantic-comedy term 'meet cute' un-ironically to describe two middle-aged business men meeting at a bar — and Michael is fully on board with this framing
jokes.explanation: The 'meet cute' framing for a business handoff is a solid joke — two men treating their coincidental meeting like a romcom setup. Works primarily because of D'Angelo's self-delusion matching Michael's.

jokes.text: D'Angelo pulls out a business card as proof of identity, calling himself the 'office funny guy' after Michael one-ups him with a funnier story
jokes.setup: Michael retells the meet-cute story; D'Angelo tries to top it with his own observation about carrying business cards
jokes.punchline: Office labels him 'office funny guy,' but D'Angelo insists he 'wasn't even trying to make a joke' — revealing someone who takes their own quirkiness very seriously
jokes.explanation: Establishes D'Angelo's self-image as an 'offbeat, twisted' guy — a character beat more than a joke, but it has comedic value in showing his obliviousness to how he's being received.

jokes.text: D'Angelo introduces Jim and Pam as 'Jap' — 'Jim and Pam, aka JAP.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is meeting the staff and introduces the couple
jokes.punchline: He combines their names into the acronym 'JAP' — apparently without awareness of the slur — as a cutesy couple nickname, creating immediate cringe
jokes.explanation: A cringe-comedy moment that works by showing D'Angelo's cluelessness immediately after he's been established as someone who thinks of himself as funny and cool. The joke is entirely in the audience's discomfort, not in what D'Angelo intended.

jokes.text: D'Angelo: 'What started as an affair has blossomed into a family before our eyes.' / Jim and Pam correct him, and D'Angelo doubles down: 'Yes, it was.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is narrating Jim and Pam's relationship history to their faces
jokes.punchline: He insists their relationship started as an affair — Jim and Pam correct him, but D'Angelo won't back down — showing his confidence is completely unjustified by his actual knowledge
jokes.explanation: D'Angelo confidently asserting wrong facts about people he just met — and not backing down when corrected — is a strong character-comedy beat. The 'yes it was' against Jim and Pam's gentle pushback is uncomfortable and funny.

jokes.text: Pam: 'We just have the one [child], but she poops for four.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo mentions he has four kids; Pam is trying to bond with him by relating
jokes.punchline: Pam's oversharing about her baby's bowel capacity as a bonding point with the new boss
jokes.explanation: A solid joke — the social awkwardness of oversharing baby details to a brand new boss is relatable and the specific detail ('she poops for four') is earthy and specific enough to be funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Yeah, they don't ever talk about careers that were made because of unplanned pregnancies, so.'
jokes.setup: Pam has just used their baby as a conversation starter with the new boss
jokes.punchline: Jim drily notes that 'careers made by unplanned pregnancies' is an underreported phenomenon — self-deprecatingly acknowledging their own situation
jokes.explanation: Pure Jim Halpert — the wry, self-aware talking head that punctuates the scene. The joke works because it's both self-deprecating and perceptive, and it's delivered in Jim's trademark deadpan. 'So.' as the trailing word is perfect economy.

jokes.text: Michael lures Dwight out with the promise of a turtle ('I would come anywhere to see a turtle') — but there is no turtle
jokes.setup: Michael needs to talk to Dwight privately and texts him to meet him
jokes.punchline: Michael lured Dwight with a fake turtle, and Dwight's enthusiastic 'I would come anywhere to see a turtle' reveals his genuine and total sincerity about turtles
jokes.explanation: Dwight's unconditional enthusiasm for turtles ('I would come anywhere to see a turtle') is perfectly in character and deeply funny. Michael knowing that a turtle is the one guaranteed lure for Dwight speaks to their relationship. The 'no turtle' reveal is satisfying.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Now I'm gonna have to go online and look at turtles, or else I'm gonna be off the whole day.'
jokes.setup: Michael reveals there's no turtle; he just used it as a lure
jokes.punchline: Dwight's coping mechanism for turtle-disappointment is to browse turtle images online — stated as a practical necessity, not an indulgence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The specificity is everything — not just 'I'm disappointed,' but a concrete, procedural response to the emotional disappointment of no turtle. 'Or else I'm gonna be off the whole day' treats turtle-browsing as essential self-care, which is both absurd and completely believable for Dwight. High originality, excellent character integration — only Dwight Schrute could deliver this line.

jokes.text: D'Angelo eating a single apple at his desk: 'I do a lot of portion control. Try to keep my daily caloric intake under 1,200.' / 'D'Angelo, you're going to starve to death.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is eating what appears to be a single apple for a meal
jokes.punchline: He reveals he caps himself at 1,200 calories — borderline starvation-level — and Michael's blunt 'you're going to starve to death' is the honest straight-man response
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — D'Angelo's extreme portion control is a funny quirk that sets him apart from Michael. Michael's straightforward 'you're going to starve to death' plays against his usual sycophancy.

jokes.text: Michael walks past a group of people eating: 'So you decided to have an orgy and not invite me? Come on! I call middle.'
jokes.setup: Several office workers are eating lunch together at their desks
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets a group lunch as an orgy, insists he should have been invited, and stakes out his preferred position ('I call middle')
jokes.explanation: 'I call middle' is the specific detail that elevates this from a generic inappropriate-workplace-comment joke to something funnier. The commitment to the bit — not just saying 'orgy' but staking out a logistics preference — is pure Michael Scott. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jim says 'It's one of my favorite regions' about the southwest and immediately cringe-checks himself in confessional: 'Did I just sound totally lame? No. I sounded good.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to bond with D'Angelo over the southwest, clearly performing enthusiasm he doesn't fully feel
jokes.punchline: He catches himself saying 'one of my favorite regions' — an oddly formal phrase — and then in talking head convinces himself it sounded fine
jokes.explanation: A good Jim moment — he's usually the show's confident straight man, so seeing him anxiously audition for the new boss and immediately doubt himself is character growth played for comedy. The self-reassurance 'No. I sounded good.' is the right note.

jokes.text: D'Angelo corrects Andy about the Grand Canyon's north rim: 'Along the north rim of the Grand Canyon is a forest as lush as you've ever seen.' / 'Burned. It's lush, dummy.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to bond with D'Angelo over the southwest but says something vaguely condescending
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo corrects him with a geographic factoid, then immediately calls him 'dummy' — an oddly aggressive move for a new manager bonding with staff
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from genuine nature appreciation to casually calling someone 'dummy' is a funny character beat for D'Angelo — it hints at a temper or social obliviousness underneath the polished exterior. Good character establishment.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'D'Angelo, I forget, did you mention you liked politics? Because I was thinking, you should meet my boyfriend. He's a state senator. I really think the two of you would hit it off. He's a great person to know.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is meeting office staff and trying to find common ground
jokes.punchline: Oscar immediately pivots to networking through his senator boyfriend — name-dropping in the most transparent career-advancement way possible, framed as a favor
jokes.explanation: A recurring joke in the season about Oscar's senator boyfriend — Oscar's transparent networking instinct is a good character beat but this particular instance isn't the sharpest execution.

jokes.text: D'Angelo tells Erin to stop saying her name when answering the phone; the subsequent exchange degrades into total indecision for 45 seconds, with D'Angelo unable to commit to any preference
jokes.setup: D'Angelo tries to exercise managerial authority by telling Erin not to say her name when answering
jokes.punchline: The entire conversation spirals into D'Angelo being unable to commit to any position — 'I sort of like the old way.' / 'Well, you know, whatever.' / 'What do you think?' — a manager incapable of managing
jokes.explanation: A sustained cringe bit that establishes D'Angelo's central flaw as a manager — he wants to assert authority but immediately caves to any pushback. The escalating wishy-washiness ('I've gotta start doing some managing at some point, right?') is very funny because he's the one undermining himself. Good structural escalation.

jokes.text: Cut to D'Angelo in a talking head: 'Change it.' — after the entire phone-answering debate ended inconclusively
jokes.setup: D'Angelo spent 45 seconds unable to make a decision about phone etiquette in front of Erin
jokes.punchline: Talking head: 'Change it.' — finally decisive, but only when he's alone and it's too late to matter
jokes.explanation: Two words. This is one of the episode's best structural jokes — the entire meandering conversation is the setup, and the payoff is D'Angelo being completely decisive in his confessional, alone, where it's meaningless. The mockumentary form is used perfectly: the talking head creates the ironic gap between his public indecision and private certainty. Economy score is perfect — two words could not do more work.

jokes.text: Erin's talking head: 'I'm so sorry. Sorry.' — reacting to the phone conversation
jokes.setup: The entire phone debate was kicked off by D'Angelo correcting Erin's phone manner
jokes.punchline: Erin apologizes — for what, exactly, is unclear — but her reflexive apologizing encapsulates her character perfectly
jokes.explanation: A character beat more than a joke — Erin's endless apologizing is on-brand but the joke itself is fairly thin. Works as a grace note after the longer bit.

jokes.text: D'Angelo summons Andy to 'make him laugh' during a mid-day lull — 'What do you got? I can't even look at you.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo has decided Andy is the 'funny guy' and wants on-demand comedy
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo is already laughing before Andy says anything ('I can't even look at you') — the absurd setup of a manager demanding comedy from an employee
jokes.explanation: The premise of a manager demanding comedy from an employee on command is inherently uncomfortable and funny. 'I can't even look at you' — laughing at Andy before he's said anything — establishes D'Angelo's weird dynamic with Andy.

jokes.text: Andy begins a joke: 'Okay, what do, um, African-Americans call the...' — then trails off into an uncomfortable pause as he realizes where he's headed
jokes.setup: Andy is on the spot to perform comedy for D'Angelo and begins a joke
jokes.punchline: The joke clearly has a racial punchline Andy can't finish — the silence is the joke; the audience watches him dig himself into a hole in real time
jokes.explanation: A masterful cringe moment. The joke is in what Andy doesn't say. The audience knows immediately where that joke is going, and so does Andy — his inability to finish it in front of a Black new boss is excruciating in the best possible way. The Office's cringe comedy at its finest: the awkward silence IS the joke. High character integration — Andy's social obliviousness and his desperation to please make this entirely believable.

jokes.text: D'Angelo's barber arrives mid-Andy-joke and D'Angelo says 'Put a pin on that. I can't wait to hear the punchline.'
jokes.setup: Andy is mid-terrible-joke; D'Angelo gets saved by the barber's arrival
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's 'put a pin on that, I can't wait to hear the punchline' — either genuinely oblivious to how bad the joke was going, or deliberately leaving Andy to stew — while other office members egg Andy on: 'Finish the joke, Andy'
jokes.explanation: The sustained torture of leaving Andy on the hook — 'I can't wait to hear the punchline' — while the colleagues pile on with 'Finish the joke, Andy' is exquisite cringe. D'Angelo ordering a barber to come to the office mid-meeting is its own power move that's casually hilarious.

jokes.text: Another character calls out: 'Finish the joke, Andy. What do African-Americans call? I don't know, help me.'
jokes.setup: Andy is still on the hook for his unfinished racist joke
jokes.punchline: A colleague doubles down by enthusiastically encouraging him to finish — either obliviously or maliciously — ratcheting up the cringe
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Andy joke sequence works through accumulation. This beat isn't as strong individually but contributes to the overall cringe arc.

jokes.text: Office reactions to D'Angelo getting a haircut at his desk: 'That is so badass. Just so hardcore. Yeah, very cool. Real power move.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo has had a barber brought in and is getting a shave/cut at his desk in the middle of the workday
jokes.punchline: The staff treat this mundane (if odd) indulgence as an act of executive dominance — 'power move,' 'hardcore' — revealing their complete readiness to sycophantically reframe anything the boss does
jokes.explanation: A good observational beat about workplace sycophancy. The office reflexively mythologizing the new boss's ordinary behavior is a sharp workplace satire point. Plays nicely off the Dwight-Michael dynamic we've seen for years being replicated instantly.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head about D'Angelo's barber: 'Saw a hawk today. Just sitting right there on the overpass, looking at me.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo has just had a barber show up at the office to shave him — a bizarre power-boss move
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking head doesn't comment on D'Angelo at all — he talks about a hawk he saw — suggesting the day has become so absurd that a hawk is the most grounded thing worth mentioning
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed non-sequitur talking head. Jim says nothing about D'Angelo — instead describing an unremarkable hawk sighting — which communicates volumes about how normalized the office chaos has become. The understatement is the joke. It's the kind of joke that gets funnier the more you think about it: Jim has decided a hawk is more noteworthy than his new boss getting a shave at work. Perfect economy, high originality for a reaction beat.

jokes.text: D'Angelo getting shaved by Erin while running a meeting — 'This is how we do it. Mmm. Feels nice, doesn't it?'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo has ordered a professional barber and also invited the office to watch him get shaved
jokes.punchline: He involves Erin in the shaving — having a receptionist shave the new manager — and sighs 'This is luxury' as the office looks on
jokes.explanation: The visual of a new manager getting shaved at work while staff watches is inherently funny. 'This is luxury' while a receptionist shaves you in a paper office is great character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael: 'We sort of do more of like pow-wows or whatevs.' / D'Angelo, startled: 'Okay, well, pow-wows then, fine.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo proposes 'rap sessions' with staff; Michael corrects him on office terminology
jokes.punchline: Michael corrects 'rap sessions' to 'pow-wows or whatevs' — replacing one potentially racially loaded term with another — and D'Angelo quickly backs down
jokes.explanation: Michael inadvertently correcting 'rap sessions' (casually racially charged) with 'pow-wows' (also casually racially charged) is a nice piece of oblivious irony. The 'whatevs' is a small characterization detail.

jokes.text: Pam shows D'Angelo a baby photo mid-meeting with extensive back-story; D'Angelo cuts her off: 'You know what? Enough about your baby, okay?'
jokes.setup: Pam interrupts the meeting with a baby photo and elaborate context ('she loves dogs, she calls them da-das')
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo flatly cuts her off: 'Enough about your baby, okay?' — an extremely blunt thing for a new manager to say, but also the thing everyone is thinking
jokes.explanation: D'Angelo saying what no polite person would say — 'enough about your baby' — is funny because it's the truth. Good economy. The setup of Pam's elaborate baby context ('she calls them da-das') makes the curtness of the shutoff funnier.

jokes.text: Michael starts offering suggestions in D'Angelo's meeting while getting his lips shaved: 'D'Angelo, you're going to want urgent A, urgent B, urgent C, urgent D...' / Erin: 'Michael, can you stop talking? I have to do your lips.' / Michael: 'Don't shave my lips.'
jokes.setup: Michael is being shaved while simultaneously trying to participate in D'Angelo's meeting
jokes.punchline: Erin needs to do his lips — requiring silence — and Michael's refusal ('don't shave my lips') suggests he's more worried about lip-shaving than contributing to the meeting
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of trying to talk while being shaved, combined with Michael's territorial behavior about his own meeting dynamics, is a good sustained bit. 'Don't shave my lips' is a funny non sequitur panic response.

jokes.text: Michael, getting shaved, keeps offering management suggestions in the meeting: 'I mark it urgent A, urgent B, urgent C, urgent D. Urgent A is the most important. Urgent D you don't even really have to worry about.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is trying to run a management meeting and Michael keeps inserting his own systems and suggestions
jokes.punchline: Michael's urgent-letter system is an elaborate and redundant solution to a problem (people ignoring urgent labels) that just... adds more urgent labels
jokes.explanation: Michael's system for making urgent labels more urgent by adding letters is circular and absurd in a very Michael way — he's solved nothing but is very pleased with the solution. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Barber interrupts Michael: 'Okay, um, Michael, can you stop talking now? I have to do your lips.' / Michael: 'Don't shave my lips.'
jokes.setup: Michael is mid-management suggestion when the barber needs to work on his upper lip area
jokes.punchline: The mundane interruption from the barber — the professional cutting off a manager's meeting contribution to address facial hair — and Michael's alarmed 'don't shave my lips' is the comic beat
jokes.explanation: A functional comedic beat that derives its humor from the absurdity of the shaving-during-meeting setup. 'Don't shave my lips' is a funny line but doesn't transcend the scene.

jokes.text: Andy's political joke: 'Democrats want electric cars. Republicans don't. How crazy is it that we got a car debate going on in a city known for gridlock?' — D'Angelo: 'Let's not talk politics in the office.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries a 'topical, edgy' political joke about electric cars and gridlock
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo shuts it down immediately — not because it's offensive, but because it's just not funny — while Andy is clearly proud of it
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke is that Andy's 'edgy topical joke' is actually quite lame, and D'Angelo diplomatically neutralizes it. The joke about Andy's joke not being funny is funnier than the joke itself — which is the point.

jokes.text: D'Angelo's talking head: 'I like you better as the funny guy. I wasn't taking a position. It was just sort of one of those things.'
jokes.setup: Andy's political joke was shut down; now D'Angelo explains in a confessional
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's explanation is barely an explanation — 'it was just sort of one of those things' — revealing he just said what he had to say and has no deeper analysis
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat — D'Angelo's non-explanation is on-brand but this particular confessional is one of the weaker ones. Doesn't add much beyond restating the previous scene.

jokes.text: Visual gag: D'Angelo laughing uproariously at something on his computer; cuts to — apparently it's a visual of someone walking, possibly a video of walking
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is laughing intensely at his computer screen; the other characters look over
jokes.punchline: What he's laughing at appears to be something mundane ('You walk much? Yeah! Right?') — his humor is completely idiosyncratic and inaccessible to others
jokes.explanation: D'Angelo's totally idiosyncratic sense of humor — laughing hysterically at something no one else understands — is a nice character beat that deepens his weirdness. Good visual gag inferred from the dialogue reactions.

jokes.text: D'Angelo unpacks office decorations: a ten-gallon hat. Michael notes: 'Technically, it only holds about three quarts. Little factoid.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo unpacks Southwest-themed office decorations including a ten-gallon hat
jokes.punchline: Michael volunteers the trivia that a ten-gallon hat only holds about three quarts — a completely unnecessary factoid delivered with smug satisfaction
jokes.explanation: Michael's random trivia-dropping ('little factoid') is a recurring trait that works here as a small character moment. The factoid itself is genuine — ten-gallon hats do only hold a fraction of ten gallons — which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: D'Angelo's talking head: 'D'Angelo's great. I love the guy. But I'm not sure he's a good fit for the office. And also, I'm not sure if I love the guy.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been enthusiastically embracing D'Angelo all episode
jokes.punchline: In his confessional, Michael retracts both statements he just made — undercutting 'D'Angelo's great' and 'I love the guy' in the same breath — revealing his ambivalence
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-contradicting talking head is a showcase of the mockumentary form. He literally walks back both of his opening statements in one breath. The pause between 'I love the guy' and 'And also, I'm not sure if I love the guy' is timed perfectly. Strong economy, high character integration — Michael's need to seem enthusiastic before admitting his doubts is entirely him.

jokes.text: D'Angelo gives money to a departing employee, then when another person approaches: 'Naw, I'm good. Keep that.' — waving off the interaction
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is interacting with staff, apparently giving out cash tips
jokes.punchline: He tips one person and then immediately doesn't tip the next person — arbitrary generosity that reveals his decision-making is completely random
jokes.explanation: A brief character beat about D'Angelo's arbitrary social behavior — giving money to one person and refusing the next. Mildly funny but not sharply constructed.

jokes.text: Andy attempts to do comedy for D'Angelo again — this time physically — but the scene is entirely silent for 20+ seconds
jokes.setup: D'Angelo again summons Andy for comedy ('What you got for me? Make me laugh.')
jokes.punchline: The transcript shows nearly 30 seconds of silence/no dialogue — suggesting Andy is performing some kind of physical bit that goes on painfully long without words
jokes.explanation: The silence itself is the joke — Andy performing something desperate and physical while D'Angelo presumably watches. The prolonged gap in dialogue creates anticipation and discomfort. Strong running gag callback. Low quotability since nothing is said, but high rewatch bonus for the visual element.

jokes.text: 'That's hot coffee! Drink some soap.' / (Pause) / 'Drink some hand soap.'
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently done something physical involving hot coffee — possibly poured it on himself or done a gag involving it
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's cure for hot coffee is 'drink some soap' — an entirely non-medical, absurd remedy — and then the clarification 'drink some hand soap' makes it worse
jokes.explanation: An excellent absurdist joke. D'Angelo's prescribed remedy for scalding — 'drink some soap' — is completely wrong and delivered with the confidence of medical advice. The follow-up specification 'drink some hand soap' makes it funnier because the clarification is still completely insane. Why hand soap specifically? The confidence and specificity elevate what could be a throwaway line into something genuinely memorable. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'I guess this is my life now.' / Then he asks D'Angelo how to become a manager at Sabre
jokes.setup: Dwight has been passed over for manager again and is resigned to his fate
jokes.punchline: 'I guess this is my life now' — Dwight's bleak acceptance of his station — followed immediately by him actively trying to change it
jokes.explanation: Dwight's resignation followed immediately by scheming is a nice character beat. 'I guess this is my life now' is bleaker than his usual bombast, which is funny in itself.

jokes.text: Dwight goes to D'Angelo to ask how to become manager. D'Angelo tells him to get a recommendation from Michael. Dwight reveals there's already one on file. D'Angelo has no idea what he's talking about.
jokes.setup: Dwight approaches D'Angelo with career ambitions
jokes.punchline: The recommendation Michael supposedly submitted turns out to not exist — the implication being Michael lied to Dwight about pushing for him, or simply never did it. D'Angelo's confusion exposes this.
jokes.explanation: A good deflating beat for Dwight. The reveal that Michael's supposed advocacy was either fictional or forgotten is a quietly sad comedy beat. D'Angelo's awkward 'I'm sorry, I never know how to act in these situations' adds a layer.

jokes.text: D'Angelo to Dwight: 'I'm so... I'm sorry, I never know how to act in these awkward-type situations.'
jokes.setup: Dwight asks about the recommendation Michael supposedly put on file — which apparently doesn't exist
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo admits he doesn't know how to handle awkward situations — which is itself delivered awkwardly — while being in an awkward situation
jokes.explanation: A mild cringe beat — D'Angelo's self-conscious acknowledgment of his own awkwardness in an awkward moment is slightly meta. Not the sharpest but functional.

jokes.text: D'Angelo on whale watching: 'If you're gonna go whale watching on the east coast, you might wanna bring a magazine called West Coast Whales. 'Cause you're not gonna see 'em.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is making conversation about regional preferences (west coast vs east coast)
jokes.punchline: His advice to east-coast whale watchers is to bring a magazine about west coast whales — so they can look at the whales they're not seeing — delivered as genuine travel advice
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly sharp piece of advice-comedy. The specificity — not just 'you won't see whales' but 'bring a magazine about the whales you're not seeing' — is the kind of absurdist-but-logical escalation that makes it work. D'Angelo delivers it with complete sincerity, as if this is useful travel advice. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Michael pulls out a peanut butter and jelly sandwich next to D'Angelo — who has a severe peanut allergy — and starts eating it
jokes.setup: D'Angelo has clearly stated he has a peanut allergy in his introduction; Michael has now appeared with a PB&J
jokes.punchline: Michael either forgot or ignored the allergy — and the entire office panics while Michael eats
jokes.explanation: The callback to D'Angelo's allergy announcement pays off well. Michael's obliviousness — or deliberate provocation — around a medical issue is very on-brand. The escalating office panic provides good comedic tension.

jokes.text: D'Angelo: 'Michael, the last time I was exposed to a peanut, I was itchy for three days, okay? Had to take baths constantly. I missed the O.J. verdict. Had to read about it in the paper like an idiot!'
jokes.setup: Michael is being scolded for bringing peanut butter near D'Angelo's allergy
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo's allergy consequences escalate from 'itchy for three days' to 'missed the O.J. verdict' — the O.J. verdict being a historically monumental TV moment that he had to read about 'like an idiot'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation structure is perfect: itchy → constant baths → missed the O.J. verdict → 'had to read about it in the paper like an idiot.' The O.J. verdict is the most-watched TV moment in American history, and D'Angelo is furious about missing it 20+ years ago because of a peanut. 'Like an idiot' is the precise detail that makes it legendary — the shame of reading about it rather than watching is treated as a genuine grievance. Comparable in spirit to the vasectomy escalation reference: unexpected, historically specific, and completely committed.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Wait. So you don't go into like shock or die or anything.' / D'Angelo: 'No, Jim. Not everything's life and death. I wanna feel comfortable.'
jokes.setup: The office has been treating D'Angelo's peanut allergy as life-threatening; D'Angelo has just revealed his allergy is actually just 'itchy'
jokes.punchline: Jim's deflating clarification question is met with D'Angelo defending his right to comfort — 'Not everything's life and death' — after the office treated this like a medical emergency
jokes.explanation: A great subversion — the audience assumed D'Angelo had a serious allergy given his emphatic introduction of it. Jim's question pops the bubble perfectly, and D'Angelo's defense — 'not everything's life and death, I wanna feel comfortable' — reveals someone who overstated their condition to get better treatment. Clean structure, excellent character integration for both Jim and D'Angelo.

jokes.text: Michael throws peanuts to Kevin and Oscar despite the allergy panic: 'I think Kevin wants one. Kevin... here ya go! Oscar, here you go!'
jokes.setup: The office is in a panic about peanuts near D'Angelo; Michael has been told to put them away
jokes.punchline: Michael ignores this entirely and starts tossing peanuts to other people — treating the allergy situation as a reason to distribute snacks, not restrict them
jokes.explanation: Michael's defiance of the peanut panic by spreading peanuts further is perfectly in character — he doesn't process the problem, he escalates it. Good physical comedy beat.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'You're getting nut particles all in the air!' / Michael: 'No one had a problem with the air here until you came around.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is alarmed about airborne peanut particles from Michael's sandwich
jokes.punchline: Michael defends the office air quality — framing Oscar's health concerns as a personal problem Oscar brought into the office
jokes.explanation: 'No one had a problem with the air here until you came around' is a quotable line that captures Michael's defensive, backwards logic perfectly. He's essentially telling D'Angelo that his allergy is the problem, not the peanuts. Strong character integration and good economy.

jokes.text: Michael locks himself in his office and shouts through the door: 'Everyone, mandatory meeting. Multipurpose room, now.' / 'No, that's good. You just stay in there. Stay in there by yourself, loser. Nobody go in.'
jokes.setup: The peanut confrontation has escalated to Michael having a territorial breakdown about his office
jokes.punchline: Michael tries to hold a rival mandatory meeting from his locked office; D'Angelo calmly tells him to stay in there and calls him a 'loser'
jokes.explanation: D'Angelo casually calling Michael a 'loser' through his own office door is a funny power dynamic reversal. Michael's territorial meeting-from-behind-a-locked-door is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Jim to Michael: 'Listen, you're the one who decided to leave. Come on. He's our new boss. You know we have to do this.' / Michael: 'Ooh, well. Who needs 'em?'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to talk Michael out of his territorial breakdown about D'Angelo
jokes.punchline: Michael's only remaining ally was Dwight — who then also abandons him — leaving Michael to say 'Who needs 'em?' to an empty hallway
jokes.explanation: Michael's bravado ('Who needs 'em?') while clearly needing them is a solid character beat. Dwight's abandonment is the more cutting element.

jokes.text: Dwight abandons Michael's rebellion and goes to D'Angelo's meeting: 'Correction. Just you.' — leaving Michael completely alone
jokes.setup: Michael assumes Dwight will be his one ally; Dwight appears to start walking to D'Angelo's meeting
jokes.punchline: 'Correction. Just you.' — Dwight's brutal, efficient abandonment of Michael
jokes.explanation: Two words with maximum impact. Dwight's 'Correction. Just you.' is devastating and funny — it uses his typically formal speech pattern ('correction') for maximum efficiency in delivering the cruelest possible message. The formality of 'correction' before the abandonment makes it funnier. Strong economy, excellent character integration — only Dwight would phrase the betrayal this way. This is one of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Michael coaches D'Angelo on how to run meetings: 'I start with some chitchat and maybe a couple of jokes.' / D'Angelo: 'And you might wanna develop a couple of characters.' / 'Go on, you'll be fine.' / 'Maybe. Maybe not. 50/50.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is nervously asking Michael how to run the office meeting; Michael offers advice
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo adds 'develop a couple of characters' as serious management advice — and his 50/50 odds assessment of success is brutally honest
jokes.explanation: The advice to 'develop a couple of characters' for office management is an absurdly theatrical recommendation that speaks to Michael's approach to leadership. D'Angelo's '50/50' self-assessment is bleakly funny.

jokes.text: D'Angelo: 'Why did you have to be so damn good?' / Michael: 'I... I'm adequate.' / D'Angelo: 'I'm half as good as you.' / Michael: 'No, no, no.'
jokes.setup: D'Angelo and Michael are having a sincere farewell moment; D'Angelo expresses admiration
jokes.punchline: Michael's self-deprecating response ('I'm adequate') — when the show has spent 7 seasons depicting his spectacular failures — is both sincere and ironic; the audience knows Michael is simultaneously less and more than he claims
jokes.explanation: Michael calling himself 'adequate' when asked why he had to be 'so damn good' is perfect character comedy — his answer is both too modest and too self-aware for Michael Scott. The emotional weight of the farewell makes the comic understatement land harder. Only Michael Scott would respond to a compliment with 'I'm adequate.'

jokes.text: Michael: 'Get your senioritis on. It's Lake Havasu time.' / D'Angelo: 'Guess I been working so hard, I... forgot what it's like to be hardly working.'
jokes.setup: Michael is encouraging D'Angelo to relax and enjoy his new position
jokes.punchline: D'Angelo delivers the old 'working hard / hardly working' wordplay — but it lands as a genuine moment of connection between the two, not just a cheap pun
jokes.explanation: The 'working hard / hardly working' pun is ancient and worn out. It lands weakly here despite the emotional context trying to give it weight. Below-average for The Office's writing standard — a lazy pun in an otherwise well-written farewell scene.

jokes.text: D'Angelo: 'What is the Native American girl's name?' — asking for the name of someone in the office, apparently
jokes.setup: D'Angelo is being helped before going into his first meeting solo
jokes.punchline: He asks for someone's name by describing them as 'the Native American girl' — revealing he has not learned anyone's name and is categorizing people by perceived ethnicity
jokes.explanation: A cringe beat that reinforces D'Angelo's cluelessness about diversity in the workplace — he's identifying staff by ethnic category rather than learning names. Consistent with his character but not the sharpest execution of the bit.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam scheme to get D'Angelo to meet baby Cece; D'Angelo meets her: 'That's a cute baby. Very cute baby. Adorable, very cute.' / Then private talking head: 'I'm telling you, that baby could be the star of a show called Babies I Don't Care About.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam engineer a situation where D'Angelo meets Cece, expecting him to be charmed; he performs enthusiasm in person
jokes.punchline: Talking head: 'That baby could be the star of a show called Babies I Don't Care About' — D'Angelo's fake enthusiasm is revealed as completely hollow; the fake show title is a perfectly calibrated insult
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. The structural payoff is excellent: Jim and Pam think they've won by getting D'Angelo to meet Cece, we see D'Angelo perform enthusiasm ('adorable, very cute'), and then the talking-head reveal is devastating. The fake show title — 'Babies I Don't Care About' — is inspired: it's specific, it's mean, and the phrase 'babies I don't care about' (plural) suggests a whole taxonomy of babies he doesn't care about, of which Cece is merely one. Perfect callback to the baby-cutoff scene. Economy is near-perfect.

tmdb_overview: The new manager, Deangelo Vickers, has everyone hoping to make good first impressions: Andy finds himself awkwardly typecast while Jim and Pam worry that they've come on too strong. Only Dwight is apathetic about the new leader.
